results.title: Beyond the brand deal: The changing business of building creator careers
results.description: As digital creators expand into acting, entertainment, entrepreneurship and original IP, the role of talent management is evolving too. With careers no longer defined by a single platform or profession, agencies such as Creators@Collective are approaching representation with a longer-term view. A creator today could negotiate a brand collaboration one day, audition for a streaming series the next, and develop an original show or consumer brand somewhere in between. As digital talent expands into entertainment, entrepreneurship and production, the business of managing that talent is becoming considerably more complex. For talent management agencies, the focus on securing brand partnerships is no longer necessarily enough. As creators explore opportunities across industries and spectrums, the expectations from representation are also expanding to include career development, creative opportunities and balancing immediate commercial returns against longer-term ambitions. But what does building a creator's career actually involve? And how much responsibility can a management agency take for that trajectory? For years, the creator economy has largely been measured through visibility, engagement, follower counts and brand collaborations. These metrics continue to play an important role, but they don't necessarily capture the full scope of what a creator can build. An audience developed through comedy, fashion, beauty or lifestyle content can also become the starting point for opportunities in entertainment, business and original storytelling. Unlike traditional actors, musicians or television personalities, digital creators often build their audiences before entering the industries they eventually want to explore. They arrive with a recognisable voice, an existing community and a degree of creative independence, but may still need to establish themselves in entirely different professional environments. This creates a different set of expectations from talent management. Finding opportunities remains important, but so does understanding which opportunities align with a creator's strengths, how different professional ambitions can coexist, and what it takes to build a career that doesn't depend on a single platform or content format. This shift also brings the creator economy closer to the fundamentals of traditional talent management, where representation has historically involved career development, professional positioning and navigating opportunities across different stages of an individual's journey. Creators@Collective is one example of how that thinking is moving into digital talent management. Drawing from a legacy of traditional entertainment representation, the agency has extended that approach to creators, digital personalities, entertainers and storytellers. Its stated philosophy centres on looking beyond talent's immediate commercial opportunities and identifying the different directions their careers could take. Its roster offers a glimpse into what that can look like in practice. From creators exploring scripted entertainment and original formats to those building consumer businesses or strengthening communities around distinct identities, their professional journeys vary. And perhaps that is the larger point: building a creator's career does not necessarily mean taking everyone down the same path. When a Creator's Career Becomes Bigger Than Their Content For a long time, creators were largely identified by the categories of content they produced. Comedy, fashion, beauty, lifestyle and entertainment were not just content genres but often became the boundaries within which their commercial opportunities were imagined. Those boundaries are becoming increasingly fluid. A comedy creator can also be an actor. A digital storyteller can move into writing or directing. Someone who has built a community around beauty or personal experiences may eventually develop a business that exists independently of their social media presence. Within Creators@Collective's roster, these different possibilities are reflected in the journeys of creators such as Dolly Singh, Srishti Garg and Sahiba Bali. Dolly Singh's career, for instance, has moved across comedy, fashion, acting and narrative storytelling. Having built a recognisable voice through digital content, she has continued to explore ways of expressing that creative identity across different formats. Her experimentation with microdrama is particularly relevant as the lines between social media content and scripted entertainment grow less rigid. For Srishti Garg, the creative process extends beyond appearing in front of the camera. Alongside acting, her work spans writing, directing and production, reflecting an interest in participating in storytelling at different stages. Her trajectory also reflects a broader shift among digital-first talent, where creators increasingly want a role in shaping the narratives they are part of, rather than being limited to performing in them. Sahiba Bali's career, meanwhile, brings together acting, sports presenting, podcasts and original formats. These are different professional spaces, but they are connected by her ability to engage audiences through performance, conversation and storytelling. Her journey reflects how a creator's interests and personality can become the foundation for work that moves across formats and industries. What connects these trajectories is not a shared definition of success, but the different ways in which creators are exploring their capabilities beyond the content that initially established their identity. For talent management, that creates a more layered responsibility. Understanding someone's existing audience remains important, but so does recognising the capabilities, interests and ambitions that may not be immediately apparent from their social media presence. When Influence Extends Into Entertainment, Entrepreneurship and Community While some creators are expanding their work through storytelling and performance, others are building professional identities that bring together entertainment, commercial partnerships, entrepreneurship and community. These journeys reflect an important distinction within the creator economy: diversification does not necessarily mean moving away from content creation. In many cases, the audience and identity established online remain central even as creators take on new roles. For Rida Tharana, that expansion has taken several forms. Her win alongside Krystle D'Souza on Prime Video's The Traitors Season 2 brought her into a different entertainment format. Her campaigns with Lux and Indie Wild, alongside associations with Louis Vuitton, H&M and Mercedes-Benz, reflect her presence across fashion, beauty and lifestyle. Beyond these, her entrepreneurial interests, including Her Circle Co., Women's First Foundation and her saree brand Nari, point to initiatives that extend beyond conventional influencer partnerships. Parul Gulati's journey offers another intersection between acting and entrepreneurship. Alongside her screen career and appearance on The Traitors, she has built Nish Hair into a consumer business. Her appearance on Shark Tank India brought her entrepreneurial journey to a wider audience, while her brand has also become closely associated with her public identity. That overlap was particularly visible during her 2025 Cannes Film Festival debut, where she wore a custom outfit incorporating hair extensions as a reference to Nish Hair. The moment brought together her identity as an actor, entrepreneur and public personality, demonstrating how the different aspects of a creator's professional life can intersect. Her premium beauty and fashion associations sit alongside these pursuits. Not every creator's growth, however, is defined by entering a new industry. Prableen Kaur Bhomrah has built her identity around beauty, body positivity and inclusivity. Her work reflects the role that community and representation can play in shaping a creator's career. In categories where personal experience, trust and identity are closely connected, the relationship between a creator and their audience can be as significant as the reach of an individual piece of content. For talent management agencies, these trajectories present different considerations. Supporting an entrepreneurial venture, navigating opportunities in mainstream entertainment and developing partnerships around a community-led identity require different approaches. The common challenge is understanding what makes each creator distinctive and which opportunities are relevant to their ambitions. The Place of Brands in a Creator's Evolving Career Even as creators explore entertainment and entrepreneurship, brand collaborations continue to be an important part of the ecosystem. They provide commercial opportunities, help creators reach new audiences and, in some cases, allow them to explore ideas and formats they may not otherwise have the resources to pursue. What is changing is the context in which these partnerships are considered. When a creator's work spans different industries, a brand deal is no longer necessarily an isolated transaction. It can become part of a broader professional identity, where the nature of the association matters alongside its commercial value. Ahsaas Channa, for example, has a career rooted in acting, with her screen portfolio spanning digital entertainment and scripted productions. Projects including Mismatched Season 4, Asur 3 and Netflix's Greater Kalesh, in which she plays a lead role, reflect her continued focus on performance. Alongside her entertainment work, she has maintained a long-term association with Nivea and participated in campaigns for Clinique. Her trajectory demonstrates how brand partnerships can coexist with an established acting career without necessarily becoming its defining feature. For Apoorva Mukhija, popularly known as The Rebel Kid, her candid storytelling, personal experiences and distinct Gen Z appeal have been central to building her digital identity. That recognisability has translated into opportunities across entertainment, including The Traitors and JioHotstar's Spice It Up, as well as collaborations spanning Nike, Meta, Amazon, Maybelline, Google, Spotify and Aqualogica. Her career also reflects how a creator's personality and relationship with their audience can become relevant across different commercial and entertainment contexts. For agencies such as Creators@Collective, the question is not simply how many partnerships a creator can secure, but how those opportunities fit into the larger direction of their career. A partnership may make commercial sense, but other considerations matter too. Does it align with the creator's public identity? Does it introduce them to a relevant audience? Does it offer creative possibilities beyond conventional campaign deliverables? And does it leave room for the creator to pursue other professional interests? As creators take on multiple professional identities, these decisions become a more significant part of talent management. What Does Long-Term Talent Management Actually Involve? Managing brand collaborations requires one set of capabilities. Navigating acting opportunities, developing original IP, exploring production partnerships or supporting entrepreneurial ambitions can involve very different considerations. There are questions around creative control, intellectual property, commercial negotiations, professional positioning and, perhaps most importantly, timing. An opportunity that makes sense for one creator at a particular stage of their career may not be equally relevant to another. This is where Creators@Collective draws on the principles of traditional talent representation. The agency describes its approach as one focused on understanding individual strengths and ambitions, working with a selective roster and considering opportunities in the context of a creator's longer-term professional direction. The underlying idea is that talent management cannot follow an identical framework for every creator. An actor looking to strengthen their screen portfolio may have different priorities from an entrepreneur building a consumer business or a digital storyteller interested in creating original formats. However, building a long-term career is not simply a matter of expanding into as many fields as possible. Every transition brings new expectations, and success in one medium doesn't automatically translate to another. A creator with a substantial online audience may still need to establish credibility as an actor. Someone building a consumer business must navigate challenges beyond personal branding. Creating original IP requires more than an audience willing to watch. For talent managers, this means understanding not only where creators could go next, but whether those opportunities match their abilities and ambitions. It also means recognising that the creator's own decisions, creative interests and willingness to experiment remain central to how their career develops. Management can identify and facilitate opportunities, but the individual ultimately shapes their career's direction. Beyond the Next Campaign As platforms, formats and audience preferences continue to evolve, the question of what makes a creator's career sustainable becomes increasingly relevant. Technology, including AI, is changing how content is developed and distributed, making production tools more accessible. But producing content and building a distinctive creative identity are not necessarily the same thing. An individual's perspective, relationship with their audience and body of work developed over time remain important factors in how their career evolves. That does not mean every creator needs to become an actor, launch a business or develop an original show. Longevity may come from exploring new industries, but it can just as easily emerge from strengthening an existing area of expertise. The larger shift lies in recognising creators as professionals whose skills and ambitions evolve, rather than viewing them primarily as channels through which brands can reach audiences. Creators@Collective's approach reflects one way the talent management business is adapting to that understanding. By bringing principles of traditional entertainment representation into the digital creator ecosystem, the agency is positioning itself around the longer arc of a creator's career, even as brand partnerships remain an important part of that journey. The creator economy may have grown around platforms, followers and collaborations, but the careers emerging from it are becoming increasingly difficult to fit into those definitions. For agencies such as Creators@Collective, the opportunity lies in recognising that difference and building representation around it. As creators continue to explore new professional identities, the real test for talent management will be how effectively it supports those transitions, rather than simply how many opportunities it can secure along the way. results.title: British jets join French nuclear exercise for first time, France says
results.description: In a significant show of solidarity, British and French military jets have engaged in a collaborative exercise aimed at enhancing their nuclear capabilities amid rising threats in Europe. Named 'Rummy', this operation involved British Typhoons and French Rafales simulating a nuclear strike. French officials stress the critical nature of their nuclear partnership in bolstering European security, underscoring their dedicated efforts to peace through robust deterrence strategies.
